# Where dplR Comes From

:::{.callout-note title="Draft"}
First draft, 2026-10-19. Replaces the 2022 Welcome; the setup material moved to the [Setup appendix](A1PackagesUsed.qmd). History is checked against @Holmes1983, @GrissinoMayer2001 and the Fortran in `legacyCode`, and against what Ed Cook told me.
:::

## Big Idea

Every number a tree-ring program hands you rests on choices somebody made. How stiff a spline to fit. Whether to take logs. Which kind of correlation, which kind of mean, how long a segment. For about forty years most of those choices lived inside Fortran programs written by a small number of people who knew the wood and knew the math. COFECHA and ARSTAN are the famous ones. They are where the field's methods were worked out, and `dplR` carries a great many of the same ideas. Its name, the Dendrochronology Program Library in R, is a nod to the library of programs Richard Holmes built.

The difference is where the choices sit. In COFECHA a choice was a prompt you answered or a constant in the source. In `dplR` it is an argument with a default, and you can see it, change it and write down what you changed. Most of the book is about those arguments: what each one does to your data, and when you'd want something other than the default.

This chapter is the short history behind that, and one example of why it matters.

## Packages

```{r}
#| label: lineage-setup
library(dplR)
```

## The Programs Before dplR

Crossdating was done by eye long before it was done by computer, with skeleton plots and by matching ring patterns from memory [@Holmes1983]. Douglass held to the rule that the wood decides the dating [@Douglass1941]. A correlation could help, but it couldn't overrule the rings.

Computers came in slowly. Holmes [-@Holmes1983] describes a routine from Fritts in 1963 that correlated an undated series with a chronology at every possible position. It worked when the dating was clean. A missing ring blurred the peak, and the routine couldn't tell you where in a series the problem was.

Holmes's answer was COFECHA, an invented Spanish word for "co-date". The first version appeared early in 1982 [@GrissinoMayer2001]. It cut each series into overlapping segments and correlated each one against a master built from the other series, so a dating error showed up as a run of weak segments starting where the error was. Holmes wrote it at the Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research in Tucson and at IANIGLA in Mendoza, Argentina [@Holmes1983]. COFECHA was one of a set of programs Holmes wrote that shared Fortran routines for reading files, asking for options and printing output. That set is the Dendrochronology Program Library, the DPL, and for years it was handed out from the lab's server [@GrissinoMayer2001].

Ed Cook's ARSTAN did for standardization what COFECHA did for dating. It fits growth curves, turns ring widths into indices, builds the chronology with a robust mean, and models the persistence in it. It carries much of the thinking in Cook's dissertation [@cook1985] and in the Cook Book [@CookBook], and Ed has kept it going ever since. The copy he gave me has a log of changes from 2006 to 2019, including an age-dependent spline added in 2014. That spline is in `dplR` too, as `ads`.

I started `dplR` around 2006 [see @Bunn2008; @Bunn2010]. A lot of it began as an attempt to do in R what those programs did, and some of the finer points of ARSTAN came from locking Ed in a conference room in 2022 (see the [Acknowledgements](A3Acknowledgements.qmd)). Richard Holmes is no longer with us. His programs are still in use, and the field still runs on his ideas.

## A Default Is a Judgment Call

Here is one choice and how it moved. Before COFECHA correlates anything, it takes the slow wiggles out of each series with a smoothing spline. A shared age trend would make every series look like it matches every other one at almost any lag. How stiff should that spline be?

In 1983 Holmes used a 20-year spline. He had tried different lengths on collections from California, and 20 years found the errors without flagging many segments that were fine. A stiffer spline left too much slow variation in, and a more flexible one flagged good segments [@Holmes1983, p. 72]. By 2001 the default was 32 years. In data sets from several regions it usually did the best job of finding errors, and it gave the highest interseries correlations [@GrissinoMayer2001, p. 207]. Same author, same program, a different answer. Both were reasonable. They came from different collections.

Other choices moved too. The 1983 paper describes a spline, a log transform and the correlation, and says nothing about autoregressive modeling. By the 2002 source, COFECHA prewhitens each series with an AR model before correlating. Ed Cook told me he talked Holmes into adding the AR step, and an option for Spearman's rank correlation. He also argued against the log transform as a default, since it skews the indices and needs a made-up constant for zero-width rings. Holmes kept it. Ed's verdict: "Not good in my opinion." Even the best disagree from time to time.

So what does `dplR` do? It depends which function you ask.

```{r}
#| label: lineage-defaults
dating <- data.frame(
  `function` = c("xdate.report", "corr.rwl.seg"),
  spline = c(deparse(formals(xdate.report)$nyrs),
             deparse(formals(corr.rwl.seg)$nyrs)),
  correlation = c(eval(formals(xdate.report)$method)[1],
                  eval(formals(corr.rwl.seg)$method)[1]),
  prewhiten = c(formals(xdate.report)$prewhiten,
                formals(corr.rwl.seg)$prewhiten),
  check.names = FALSE
)
dating
```

`xdate.report` follows COFECHA, with a `r formals(xdate.report)$nyrs`-year spline and `r tools::toTitleCase(eval(formals(xdate.report)$method)[1])`'s correlation, so people coming from COFECHA see familiar numbers. `corr.rwl.seg` is older. With `nyrs = NULL` it divides each series by its mean and leaves the AR model to take out the persistence, and it uses `r tools::toTitleCase(eval(formals(corr.rwl.seg)$method)[1])`'s rank correlation. Neither takes logs. Both prewhiten, which is Ed's step.

Neither set of defaults is the right one. They are two sensible answers to the same question, and the crossdating chapters show you how to tell when the choice changes what gets flagged. And you can see them. To know what COFECHA was doing to your series you had to know the program well. In `dplR` you can type `formals(xdate.report)` or read the help page, and if you change something, the change is in your script for anyone to see.

## Scripture

ARSTAN, COFECHA and the DPL are the field's scripture. When you want to know why a method exists, or why it has the default it has, they're where to look, along with the papers that described them. I cite them throughout the book and tell their history where it explains something.

They aren't the test of whether `dplR` is right, though. I spent a lot of time tuning `dplR` to reproduce COFECHA and ARSTAN number for number, and I've stopped. Those programs made choices for you, which made sense before anyone had an IDE. In R you can make them yourself. Where `dplR` does something different, the book says what it does, why, and which argument gets you the older behavior.

## The Neighborhood

`dplR` isn't the only R package for tree rings. There are `measuRing` for measuring, `detrendeR` for detrending, `burnr` for fire history, `TRADER` and `dfoliatR` for disturbance and insect outbreaks, `treeclim`, `pointRes` and `dendroTools` for climate and growth, `dendrometeR` and `dendRoAnalyst` for dendrometer data, and `xRing` and `RAPTOR` for wood density and cell anatomy, and more besides. The book uses a few of them where `dplR` stops. There is also a Python port, `dplPy`, which gets [its own chapter](17DplPy.qmd).

## Citing dplR

Cite the software you use. It tells a reader exactly what you ran, and when results differ between versions, the version number is how anyone tracks it down. R will tell you how:

```{r}
#| label: lineage-cite
citation("dplR")
```

`citation()` with no argument gives you R itself, and the same call works for any package. The R Core Team asks that you cite R when you use it for data analysis, and so do I. Writing `dplR` has been an act of love. But I am not among the idle rich, and neither is anybody else who has worked on it. We have jobs and occasionally have to answer to our betters. When a department chair or a dean accuses us of being dilettantes, your citation is a partial excuse.

## Wrapping Up

`dplR` grew out of COFECHA, ARSTAN and the DPL, and it keeps most of their methods. What it changes is where the choices live. A spline length or a correlation method is an argument you can read, change and record, and the defaults are judgment calls that someone else could reasonably make differently. Even `dplR`'s own dating functions disagree.

None of this tells you which choice is right for your collection. That depends on the data, and finding out is most of what the rest of the book does. The [next chapter](02CoresToRecord.qmd) starts by asking what a ring width is made of.

## Exercises

1. Run `corr.rwl.seg(wa082, make.plot = FALSE)` with the default `nyrs = NULL`, then with `nyrs = 20` and `nyrs = 32`. How many series are flagged each time? What would you need to know to say which run is right?
2. Look up `nyrs` in `?detrend`. What spline stiffness do you get when it is `NULL`? Find where that rule comes from in the Cook Book [@Cook1990, p. 114].
3. Plant a missing ring with `bad <- delete.ring(co021, series = "643143", year = 1600)`, then run `xdate.report(bad)` with `method = "pearson"` and with `method = "spearman"`. Does the choice change what gets flagged at Mesa Verde? Try the same thing on a `wa082` series. Do you expect a difference there?
4. Run `citation()` for `dplR` and for one other package you use. What would you put in a methods section?

## Further Reading

- @Holmes1983 is COFECHA's first description, and it is short. Read it for why the spline and the segments are there, and for Holmes's account of testing spline lengths on California collections.
- @GrissinoMayer2001 is the COFECHA manual most people learned from. It walks through every option and every part of the output, and it is the best guide to what `xdate.report` is imitating.
- @CookBook is where ARSTAN's methods are written out at length: growth curves, the biweight mean and the AR model of a chronology. Chapter 3 is the one to have on your desk.
- @cook1985 is Ed Cook's dissertation, the source of much of that chapter and of how `dplR` standardizes.
- @Douglass1941 is Douglass on why the wood decides the dating.
